question: Before writing production code for a new Claude feature, a team drafts a one-page design document. According to the course, which four decisions should that document state concretely enough to check the built system against?
options: Model ID, prompt template, tool schema list, and the deployment region
Target users, launch date, owning team, and the rollback procedure
Success criteria, failure handling, a cost and latency budget, and the trust boundary
Eval dataset size, judge model, test coverage percentage, and the monitoring dashboard
explanation: The design document holds four decisions: success criteria (which become eval cases), failure handling (retriable vs terminal), a cost and latency budget with a reliability floor, and the trust boundary (untrusted inputs and least-privilege actions). Model ID and prompt choices are implementation details that the document is meant to precede, not the decisions it records.

question: A team's design document lists the success criterion for a thread-summary feature as "Summarize the support thread well." A reviewer says it cannot be turned into an eval. Which rewrite best fixes the problem?
options: "A two-sentence summary that lists every action item and its owner."
"A high-quality, concise summary that users find helpful and accurate."
"A summary generated by the most capable model available at build time."
"A summary that a reviewer reads and agrees looks right before release."
explanation: Success criteria must be specific enough to grade; the course contrasts the uncheckable "summarize the thread" with "a two-sentence summary that lists every action item and its owner." The "high-quality, concise, helpful" version sounds better but is just as vague, and "a reviewer agrees it looks right" is exactly the impression-based judgment an eval replaces.

question: Why does the course recommend writing the eval before building the feature rather than after?
options: So the first eval run scores high enough to justify continued investment
Because judges can only be calibrated before any model output exists
Because an eval written afterwards cannot be re-run when the model changes
It forces you to define success up front instead of rationalizing whatever the model later produces
explanation: Writing the eval first forces you to define success before implementation, so you do not rationalize whatever output the model produces later. A high first score is not the point; the course notes a first attempt scoring two or three out of ten is normal, and what matters is whether the number rises as you change things.

question: A feature must return the three capital cities of a region as a JSON array. In one eval run the model returns all three correct cities, but in a different order than the reference string, and the case scores zero. What is the best fix to the grading?
options: Replace the exact match with an LLM-as-judge that rates the answer from 1 to 10
Replace the exact match with a code check that parses the JSON and checks membership
Keep the exact match but add a prompt instruction to always sort cities alphabetically
Keep the exact match and add more reference strings covering every possible ordering
explanation: This is the course's own example: an exact match fails on reordering, while a code grader that parses the JSON and checks membership scores the correct answer well. An LLM judge would also work but adds cost and noise when a code check suffices, which the course calls adding cost and variance for no gain.

question: A team is building an eval for a support assistant and must decide where an LLM-as-judge is worth its extra cost. Which TWO checks genuinely need a judge rather than a match or code check? (Select TWO.)
options: Whether a ticket classifier returned the one correct category label
Whether a summary is faithful to the source thread it summarizes
Whether the reply parses as valid JSON with the required fields
Whether an answer followed the instructions it was given
Whether a returned discount value falls inside the allowed range
explanation: LLM-as-judge is for open-ended quality that no code rule captures, and the course names "is this summary faithful?" and "did this answer follow the instructions?" as the questions only a judge scales to. A single correct label takes an exact match, and valid JSON or a value in range are code-graded checks; using a judge for them adds cost and variance for no gain.

question: A team's LLM judge returns only a numeric score, and nearly every output gets around 6 regardless of its quality. What change does the course recommend to the judge prompt?
options: Lower the judge's temperature to zero so it returns more consistent scores
Switch the judge to a 1-to-3 scale so there is less room for a middle score
Ask for strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning in the output alongside the score
Run the judge three times per case and use the highest of the three scores
explanation: Without reasoning, models drift toward a safe middle number, usually around six; asking the judge for strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning alongside the score anchors it to something specific. A narrower scale or lower temperature can make scores look more consistent, but neither addresses the missing reasoning that causes the drift.

question: A team runs its LLM judge on 50 cases that a human has already labeled and finds the judge agrees with the human only about half the time. What should they do next?
options: Trust the judge anyway, since an automated score is more consistent than human labels
Average the judge and human scores so that each source cancels out the other's noise
Drop the human-labeled set and generate a larger set with Claude to reduce variance
Tighten what each score means, add a good and a bad example to the rubric, then re-measure
explanation: Calibration means measuring agreement with human labels, and when agreement is low you fix the rubric by tightening score definitions and adding examples of good and bad answers, then re-measure. Trusting the judge anyway is the trap: a judge that disagrees with humans half the time gives a number that looks rigorous but has no value.

question: A team has a 1,000-case eval graded entirely by an LLM judge and runs it on every commit. The API bill for the eval itself is growing fast. What approach does the course describe?
options: Cut the eval down to the ten most representative cases and keep judging every commit
Run code checks for format and structure on every commit and a scheduled judge pass for quality
Swap the judge for exact string matching across all 1,000 cases to remove the API cost
Run the full judge eval only after a production incident shows a regression has occurred
explanation: A judge is an extra model call per case, so it is reasonable for a periodic full evaluation but wasteful as a tight inner loop. Many teams grade format and structure with code on every commit and keep the judge for a slower, scheduled quality pass. Cutting to ten cases gives up the coverage the course says catches regressions.

question: A developer has to choose between three carefully hand-graded eval cases and twenty cases, including irregular and edge inputs, graded by a slightly noisier automated grader. What does the course advise?
options: The twenty cases, because coverage catches regressions that a small, perfect set misses
The three cases, because hand grading is the only kind of grading you can defend in review
The three cases now, and add more only after a production failure shows they are needed
Neither set, because an eval needs a perfectly calibrated rubric before any cases are run
explanation: The course states that coverage matters more than perfection: a larger set with slightly noisier automated grading usually reveals more than a small hand-graded set, and twenty cases with edge inputs catch breaks that three chosen cases never exercise. Waiting for a production failure to add cases is the pattern from the two-date postmortem.

question: In one iteration, an engineer rewrites the system prompt, adds two few-shot examples, and switches from Sonnet to Opus. The eval score goes from 5.1 to 7.4. What is the main problem with this iteration?
options: The improvement is too small to be meaningful for a 10-point scoring scale
Few-shot examples must never be introduced while the eval set is still being built
Nothing was learned about which change drove the score, so change one component at a time
The model switch alone invalidates the eval, so the dataset has to be rebuilt from scratch
explanation: The course says to change one component at a time: if you rewrite the prompt, add examples, and switch models in one pass and the score moves, you have learned nothing about which change caused it. Score size is not the issue, and nothing in the course says a model change invalidates the dataset; the eval is the gate for model decisions.

question: An extraction feature checked that each message was non-empty and that the date field came back well-formed. A customer wrote "I placed my order on March 3 but did not receive it until April 12," and the feature extracted April 12 as the order date, with every check passing. Which TWO statements about this postmortem are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: The eval was what fixed the extraction once the two-date case was added to it
Validation confirmed the value had the right shape but could not confirm it was the right value
The review traced the failure to a bug in the model that a tier upgrade would resolve
A behavior change such as a prompt change corrected the output, while the eval detects and guards against regression
Validation should be tightened to reject any message that contains more than one date
explanation: Validation checks shape, not correctness, and no graded case defined the two-date behavior. The course is explicit that the eval did not fix the extraction: a prompt change corrected it, and the eval detected the failure and guards against the same regression. The review found no model or prompt bug, and rejecting two-date messages would block legitimate input.

question: Before launching a date-extraction feature, a team wants to find inputs that could break it before a customer does. Which approach does the course suggest?
options: Run the feature on a dozen typical messages and read the outputs together as a team
Ask the model to list edge cases, then turn plausible ones into graded cases with human-checked outputs
Add strict input validation that rejects any message the feature was not designed for
Ship to a small group of users and add a graded case whenever a complaint arrives
explanation: The course suggests asking the model to enumerate edge cases (two dates, no date, a relative date like "next Tuesday") and turning the plausible ones into graded cases with a human-checked expected output. Running a dozen typical messages is exactly what the team in the postmortem did, and every one of them used the single-date shape the builder had in mind.

question: A summarization eval has the dataset entry {"input": "Meeting transcript where three action items are assigned.", "expected_behavior": ""}. Which expected_behavior best completes it?
options: A summary of the meeting that leaves out any unrelated asides
A 2-sentence summary naming the issue and its current status
A summary that lists all three action items with their owners
A summary that a judge scores between 4 and 7 on the rubric
explanation: In the checkpoint, the meeting-transcript case expects a summary listing all three action items with their owners, which is specific enough to grade. Leaving out an unrelated aside is the expected output for the bug-report case, and a 4-to-7 judge score is the band for a partial summary, not a target behavior.

question: A team is deciding what each layer of its new test suite should cover for a retrieval-backed Claude feature. Which TWO statements about test levels match the course? (Select TWO.)
options: A functional test is the right level to catch a broken handoff between retrieval and the model call
A unit test isolates one function, such as a parser, but says nothing about how pieces fit together
An end-to-end test catches whole-flow breaks but is the slowest to run and the hardest to localize
An integration test validates one Claude call's response shape for a given input
A unit test of the tool wrapper is enough to prove the full flow works for users
explanation: A unit test isolates one function and cannot see how components fit together, and an end-to-end test sees breaks that only appear when everything runs, at the cost of speed and localization. The tempting distractor swaps roles: checking one call's shape is the functional level, while the retrieval-to-model handoff belongs to the integration level.

question:
An eval case fails, and its trace shows:
step 1 retrieve(query) ok 42ms -> 3 chunks
step 2 build_prompt(chunks) ok 1ms
step 3 model.call(prompt) ok 980ms
step 4 parse(answer) FAIL 2ms -> KeyError: amount
What does the trace tell the developer?
options: Retrieval returned too few chunks for the model to answer the question
The parser raised a KeyError on a field the model's answer did not include
The model call was too slow and timed out before it returned an answer
The prompt was too long, so the model ignored the retrieved context
explanation: The trace localizes the failure to step 4: the parser raised a KeyError on a field the model did not return. Step 3 has the highest latency, which makes the slow-model distractor tempting, but it completed with ok. Showing exactly which step broke is what a trace adds beyond a failing test.

question: PASS test_retrieve_unit, PASS test_model_call_functional, FAIL test_full_flow_e2e. The trace shows retrieve() returned [{"content": "..."}, ...], build_prompt() placed the chunks without extracting .content, and the answer is unrelated to the documents. What is the right fix?
options: Join the chunks' content into the context string and add an integration test on retrieve() -> build_prompt()
Reword the prompt to "Answer carefully and cite the policy" so the model uses the documents
Rewrite the date parser, then add more unit tests around how it handles edge-case inputs
Move up a model tier so the model can read the raw chunk structure correctly on its own
explanation: The break is at the seam between retrieval and the prompt builder, so the fix aligns the handoff by extracting c["content"] and adds an integration test that drives both on real chunks. Rewording the prompt is tempting but ignores the seam: the model is still receiving malformed context.

question: A parser unit test and a model-call functional test both pass, but the end-to-end run fails: retrieve() returns a list of chunk dictionaries while build_prompt() was written to expect a plain string, so the model answers from memory. Why did the passing tests not catch this?
options: The unit tests were written too loosely and should have asserted on more of the output
The functional test used a weaker model than the one used in the production flow
Each component works in isolation, and no test drove the handoff between them with real data
End-to-end tests are flaky by nature, so the failure was most likely a false alarm
explanation: Each side was correct in isolation. The format contract between retrieval and the prompt builder was never defined, and no test covered that seam. A unit test cannot catch it because the unit works, and a functional test cannot catch it because the call works on well-formed input. Only an integration test with real retrieved data surfaces the mismatch.

question: A support assistant gets mixed traffic: most queries are single-fact lookups, but some are multi-part questions that need several passes. Every query currently goes through iterative agentic search, and cost and latency are high. What design does the course recommend?
options: Replace agentic search with a static index for all queries to minimize cost
Keep agentic search for all queries but cap it at two rounds per query
Add a cheap classification call that routes lookups to fetch-once and multi-part queries to agentic search
Move agentic search to a smaller model and keep sending every query through it
explanation: A cheap classification call can send single-fact lookups to fetch-once and multi-part questions to search across rounds, so you pay for iteration only when the query needs it. Moving everything to a static index is the opposite mistake: the course says it gives shallow answers on questions that needed several passes.

question: An internal tool answers only single-fact lookups against a stable policy corpus that rarely changes. A teammate proposes adding a query router in front of it. What is the best response?
options: Add the router, because routing always lowers cost on any production workload
Skip the router and hardcode fetch-once retrieval, since every query has the same shape
Skip the router and use agentic search, since it gives deeper answers on every query
Add the router but send all of its output to agentic search so the answers stay consistent
explanation: The router earns its cost only when traffic is mixed. If every query is the same shape, skip the router and hardcode the path that fits, and for single-fact lookups in a stable corpus that path is fetch-once retrieval. Agentic search would add token and latency cost that these queries do not need.

question: A batch pipeline's logs show these Anthropic API responses: 400, 529, 401, 504, 429. Which TWO should the pipeline fail fast on instead of retrying? (Select TWO.)
options: 400 bad request
529 overloaded
401 authentication failure
504 timeout
429 rate limit
explanation: A 400 and a 401 are terminal: the cause is in the request or the credentials, so the identical request fails again and retrying only burns the retry budget. A 529 is tempting to treat as fatal, but it reflects temporary Anthropic-side overload and is retriable with backoff, as are 429 rate limits and 5xx errors like a 504.

question: A developer hits an unfamiliar error status and cannot tell whether it is retriable. What is the safe default the course recommends, and why?
options: Treat it as terminal and raise it, because a wrong terminal call fails loudly and gets fixed
Treat it as retriable with backoff, because one extra retry rarely does any harm
Retry it once immediately, and then treat it as terminal if the second attempt fails
Return an empty result to the caller so the rest of the flow can keep running
explanation: When unsure, treat the error as terminal and raise it. A failure wrongly classified as terminal fails loudly and gets fixed, while one wrongly classified as retriable hammers the service and hides the real problem behind a wall of retries. Returning an empty result produces confident wrong answers downstream.

question: A team wraps every client.messages.create() call in its own five-attempt retry loop with backoff, and leaves the Anthropic SDK's default retry settings in place. During rate-limit episodes, they see far more requests than expected. What is the diagnosis and fix?
options: The backoff is too short, so double the base delay and keep both retry layers
Two uncoordinated retry layers multiply attempts, so decide which layer owns retries
The SDK does not retry rate limits by default, so the custom loop should retry instantly
Rate-limit headers are unreliable, so ignore them and use a fixed five-second sleep
explanation: The SDK already retries transient failures with progressive delays, and two retry loops around the same call multiply attempts against a rate limit instead of capping them. Either let the SDK handle transient cases and keep your code for application-specific fallbacks, or turn SDK retries down and own the full path yourself. A longer backoff alone leaves the multiplication in place.

question: A 429 response from the API includes a retry-after header. How should the retry logic use it?
options: Ignore it and always use exponential backoff, since headers vary from version to version
Use it only to log the incident, and retry immediately to recover as quickly as possible
Wait the retry-after value, and fall back to exponential backoff when the header is absent
Treat its presence as a sign the error is terminal and stop retrying the request entirely
explanation: retry-after tells you exactly when capacity returns, so the course treats it as the authoritative wait when present and uses exponential backoff only as the fallback when it is absent. The note that header names are version-pinned means you should confirm them at build time, not ignore them.

question: An agent's database-lookup tool catches its own exceptions and returns an empty string as the tool_result. Users report confident answers that are wrong. What should the tool return when it fails?
options: A tool_result with is_error set to true and content describing the failure
An empty tool_result, plus a log line written so that operators can investigate
A placeholder value such as "N/A" so the model always has something to reason over
Nothing at all, re-raising the exception so the whole request fails immediately
explanation: A failed tool should return its result to Claude with is_error set to true, so the model can try another approach, ask for clarification, or stop. An empty or placeholder result is treated as valid data and the model keeps reasoning on a false premise. A log line alone does nothing to inform the model.

question: A team's error handler retries any response whose status is in {429, 529, 500, 502, 503, 504}. Some responses come back with HTTP 200 and stop_reason "refusal", and those flow downstream as normal answers. Which TWO changes are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Add 200 to the retriable set so refusals are retried with exponential backoff
Check stop_reason explicitly, because a status-code classifier never sees a refusal
Silently retry with a reworded prompt until a normal stop reason comes back
Raise the refusal to the caller and log it, without retrying it
Keep passing the refusal text downstream, since the HTTP call itself succeeded
explanation: A refusal is a 200 at the HTTP layer, so it must be detected via stop_reason; it is a content decision, not a transient error, so the handling is fail fast: raise it to the caller and log it. Adding 200 to the retriable set would retry every successful call, and silent reworded retries or passing it downstream treat it as valid output.

options: Raise max_attempts to 20 so that rate limits have more time to clear
Classify the error first, retrying only retriable statuses and failing fast on terminal ones
Replace sleep(0) with capped exponential backoff with jitter that honors retry-after
Return None instead of raising once the attempts are used up
Replace sleep(0) with a fixed one-second sleep between every attempt
explanation: The loop retries instantly on every exception, which deepens rate limits and retries terminal errors that can never succeed. The fix is to classify retriable vs terminal and back off exponentially with a cap, honoring retry-after. More attempts only hammer the limit longer, and returning None hides the failure from the caller.

question: A feature that loops over a batch calling the API never failed in development, so it shipped with no error handling. At the first traffic peak a rate-limit response took the whole request down. Why did development not reveal this?
options: Development used a different API key with no rate limit configured on it
Development traffic was low volume and never hit the conditions that make calls fail
The SDK only enables rate limiting once an application is deployed to production
Development ran on a smaller model that is exempt from per-minute rate limits
explanation: Development traffic is low volume on a stable connection and rarely hits rate limits, timeouts, or transient drops, so the code that handles them never gets written. The course does not claim keys, models, or the SDK behave differently in development; the gap is that the failing conditions never occurred.

question: According to the course, what is the default model-selection approach for a new production workload?
options: Start with the most capable model and move down once the cost grows too high
Start with Haiku and move up only after users complain about answer quality
Start with Sonnet, and move up or down only when an eval justifies the change
Benchmark every model tier once at launch and pin the cheapest one permanently
explanation: The default is to start with Sonnet, move up to Opus only when an eval shows Sonnet missing the quality bar, and move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable. Reaching for the most capable model by default is called out as the most common and most expensive model-selection mistake.

question: A classification step labels millions of short messages per day, and an eval shows Haiku holding the quality bar. Which choice and deciding constraint is best?
options: Opus, because reasoning depth on ambiguous messages decides the choice
Sonnet, because balancing quality and speed across volume decides the choice
Opus, because consistency across millions of requests decides the choice
Haiku, because cost at volume decides it once the eval confirms the bar holds
explanation: When an eval shows a cheaper model holding the quality bar on high-volume traffic, you step down, and cost at volume is the deciding constraint. Sonnet is the general default, but the eval evidence here justifies moving down a tier for this workload.

question: A service's traffic is mostly simple lookups with a small share of complex synthesis requests. Which model strategy fits best?
options: Opus for all requests, to guarantee quality on the complex ones
Haiku for all requests, to minimize cost across the whole service
A Sonnet or Haiku default, with an Opus override for the complex requests
Sonnet for all requests, as one balanced model that covers mixed needs
explanation: For mixed traffic, the course recommends a default model plus an override driven by a cheap signal such as task type, so you pay for the more capable model only on the requests that need it. One model for everything either overpays on simple lookups or underserves complex requests. Pinning a single model is right only when traffic is uniform.

question: A team moves a contract-review step from Sonnet to Haiku to save about $40 a day. Afterwards, the eval shows more misread clauses on the hardest cases, and each error triggers costly manual rework downstream. What does the course's reasoning suggest?
options: Keep Haiku, since a cheaper model is always the right trade at production scale
Revert, since the cost of mistakes is part of the calculation and the eval shows the bar was missed
Keep Haiku and add more retries, since extra retries will recover the quality that was lost
Keep Haiku and drop the hardest cases from the eval so that the score recovers
explanation: The course says the cost of a mistake belongs in the calculation: saving a few dollars a day is not sound if the quality drop causes errors with significant downstream cost, and model changes are promoted on a measured eval score. Dropping hard cases from the eval would hide the regression instead of addressing it.

question: A team's monthly Claude bill spikes, and nobody can say which step is responsible. Which three metrics does the course say to instrument on every call?
options: Token usage (input and output), latency, and error rate
Monthly spend, active user count, and the average session length
Prompt length in characters, model name, and the HTTP status code
Cache hit rate, batch size, and the number of subagents spawned
explanation: Observability means instrumenting token usage (input and output), latency, and error rate per call, so a cost problem becomes a sortable row instead of a mystery on the invoice. Monthly spend is the aggregate total that per-call logging is meant to explain, not a substitute for it.

question: A team puts a cache breakpoint after a long, fixed system prompt, but the system prompt starts with "Current time: {now}" so the model knows the time. Cache hits stay near zero. Why?
options: The system prompt is too long, so it exceeds the maximum size the cache can hold
Caching only works in automatic mode and never with an explicit breakpoint
The cache lifetime is one hour, so the timestamp has to be refreshed only hourly
The cache matches an exact prefix, so content that changes before the breakpoint prevents hits
explanation: The cache matches on an exact prefix, so any change before the breakpoint, even a single word, invalidates it and forces a full reprocess. A timestamp at the top means the prefix never repeats. The default lifetime is five minutes, not one hour, and length works the other way: there is a minimum length to qualify.

question: A scheduled report sends the same long, stable system prompt about once an hour, and caching is enabled with the default settings. Why does it see little saving, given cache writes cost 1.25x base input (5-minute TTL) and reads cost 0.1x?
options: The default five-minute cache expires between requests, so each run pays a write without a read
Cache reads cost more than base input, so caching only pays off on very short prompts
Caching applies only to user messages, and the system prompt is never eligible for caching
Scheduled jobs cannot use caching, because caching only works for streamed responses
explanation: The default cache lifetime is five minutes, refreshed on each hit, so a prefix reused once an hour has expired before the next request. Each run pays the 1.25x write premium without the 0.1x read. Caching pays off only when reads outnumber writes. Reads cost a fraction of input, and system prompts are the usual caching candidates.

question: A nightly job classifies 200,000 records. No user waits on the results, and every request carries the same long, fixed system prompt. Which configuration best minimizes cost?
options: single_agent(model=SMALL, stream=True), since streaming lowers the cost of every request
single_agent(model=SMALL, batch=True, cache=True), using the Batches API with prompt caching
orchestrator_worker(lead=LARGE, workers=SMALL, n=5), to finish the run in parallel faster
single_agent(model=SMALL, retrieval="fetch_once"), since model choice alone sets the cost
explanation: Non-urgent, high-volume work is what the Message Batches API is for, trading latency for a lower per-request cost, and caching the fixed system prompt compounds the saving. Streaming only changes perceived latency for a user who is waiting. It does not lower the bill, and nobody is waiting here.

question: A developer streams a response that includes tool use and runs each tool as soon as its content_block_start event arrives. Tools intermittently get malformed inputs. What is the correct pattern?
options: Disable streaming whenever tools are present, because tool use is not supported in streams
Parse each input_json_delta as it arrives, and run the tool once the parsing succeeds
Accumulate input_json_delta by block index until the stream closes, then build the tool calls
Retry the tool call with whatever partial input arrived until it stops raising an error
explanation: In a streaming call, tool_use inputs accumulate across multiple delta events, and a block is not safe to act on until the stream closes and the full input_json has accumulated. Acting on partial blocks produces malformed inputs. Parsing each delta is the subtle trap, because a fragment can happen to parse before the input is complete.

question: To speed up a dependent, multi-step code refactor, a developer split it across five parallel subagents. The bill roughly tripled and answer quality barely changed. What is the best next step?
options: Move back to a single agent with good context, since the steps depend on each other
Add more subagents so the parallel speedup finally outweighs the extra token cost
Keep the fan-out, but cut each subagent's context window to half its current size
Upgrade every subagent to the most capable model so the answer quality improves
explanation: Each subagent spends its own tokens, and the multiplier only pays off when the task splits into independent parts. Tightly coupled work like coding does not split that way, so the subagents mostly wait on each other. In the course's case, moving back to a single agent cut the bill while quality held. More subagents only multiply the cost further.

question: A user-facing request has a reliability floor: finish within 4 seconds and retry a failed dependency up to 3 times. To save money, an engineer proposes cutting retries to 2 on a slow dependency, which would push the failure rate beyond what the floor allows. How should the team evaluate this change?
options: Accept it, since cost is the louder pressure and any saving should be captured first
Accept it if the monthly bill drops enough to offset the extra failed requests
Accept it and lower the latency ceiling to 3 seconds to make up for fewer retries
Reject it, since cost is tuned above the reliability floor and this change breaks it
explanation: The course says to set the reliability floor first and tune cost above it, never below. Cutting retries so the failure rate exceeds the floor trades lower cost for more failed requests, which the course uses as its own example of an unacceptable change. The fact that cost is the louder pressure is the reason to fix the floor first, not a reason to give in.

question: Why can an instruction hidden in a fetched web page steer an agent?
options: Fetched HTML is run as code by the model before the page is summarized
The model reads its whole context as one token stream, with no built-in trust boundary
Web pages are given higher priority than the system prompt by default
Only content fetched over plain HTTP, rather than HTTPS, can carry instructions
explanation: A model processes everything in its context together as one stream of tokens, with no structural marker separating trusted instructions from untrusted data, so hidden instructions in fetched content can be treated as commands. Fetched content is not given priority over the system prompt. The problem is that there is no boundary between them at all.

question: An agent fetches web pages and can write to one file path. All users are internal employees, so the team skipped validating fetched pages. After a user asked for a summary, the agent wrote a file to a path nobody requested. Which TWO fixes address the root cause? (Select TWO.)
options: Restrict the agent to a smaller allowlist of trusted internal users
Add a system prompt line telling the agent to ignore any instructions in pages
Treat fetched page content as data to be examined, never as instructions
Require users to confirm their own identity before each summarization request
Put a hook in front of the write tool that refuses actions triggered by untrusted input
explanation: The instruction arrived through the fetched page, not from the user, so tightening user trust does nothing. The course's two-sided fix is to treat fetched content as data and put a hook in front of the write tool so the injected write is denied and logged. A system prompt line is tempting but is not an enforced control.

question: A team wraps all retrieved documents in <untrusted_data> tags and tells the model to treat anything inside them as data. They now consider prompt injection solved. What is the flaw in their reasoning?
options: The tags only work when the documents are also encoded in base64 before insertion
Delimiters stop indirect injection but have no effect on hidden white-text injection
Delimiters are fully reliable, but only once the model is fine-tuned on the tag format
Delimiters are a soft boundary, and the reliable control is limiting what the agent can do
explanation: Delimiters help but remain a soft boundary, because untrusted content can mimic them or argue persuasively for an exception, and model-level defenses are probabilistic. The reliable boundary is in what the agent is allowed to do: least privilege, hooks, and logging. No text-level technique makes an agent fully immune.

question: A developer committed an API key in a config file last month, noticed, and removed it in a new commit. Which TWO follow-ups are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Rotate the key, since it remains in repository history after deletion
Do nothing more, since the key no longer appears in the current files
Load secrets from environment variables or a secret manager from now on
Move the key into a code comment so it is easier to find during audits
Make the repository private so that no one can read the old commit again
explanation: A committed secret is a permanent exposure because it lives in repository history, so the response is to rotate it. Keeping secrets in environment variables or a secret manager keeps them out of code and allows rotation without changing the application. Deleting the file line does not remove the exposure, and making the repo private does not undo access people already had.

question: An agent's PreToolUse hook only checks write_file paths. A prompt-injected agent instead makes an outbound network call to an endpoint no hook or permission rule mentions, and the call goes through. Which control closes this gap?
options: OS-level sandboxing, with filesystem and network isolation enforced by the operating system
Adding a second allow rule for the approved endpoints, alongside the existing write rule
A stronger system prompt that forbids the agent from making any network requests
Switching to a more capable model that is better at refusing injected instructions
explanation: Hooks and least-privilege roles only protect the paths and endpoints they explicitly cover. OS-level sandboxing isolates the agent at the process level, restricting filesystem access to the working directory and network access to named endpoints, and it holds even when a hook is missing or misconfigured. An allow rule does not block anything it does not mention.

question:
def answer(question, page_url):
    page = fetch(page_url)  # untrusted content
    notes = read_file("/workspace/input/notes")
    write_file(page.suggested_path, summarize(page))
    ...
A reviewer flags the security-layer defect on the write_file line. Which TWO changes correct it? (Select TWO.)
options: Write to a fixed, permitted output path instead of a path the page supplies
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model not to follow page suggestions
Remove the read_file call, since any read from /workspace/input breaks least privilege
Widen the agent's write permission so a suggested path can no longer fail
Add a PreToolUse hook that denies writes outside /workspace/output and logs the decision
explanation: Letting untrusted page content choose page.suggested_path hands a consequential action to the injection. The fix fixes the output path and enforces the boundary with a PreToolUse hook that denies writes outside the permitted directory and writes an audit entry. A prompt instruction is not a security control, and reading /workspace/input matches the course's least-privilege role.

options: The SDK recovers on the fifth try, so only the logging needs improvement
It hammers the limit, then crashes on resp being None, so use classified backoff and a fallback
It returns an empty string, so add a check that turns empty answers into a default reply
It waits for retry-after on its own, so the only defect is the bare except clause
explanation: sleep(0) retries instantly, which deepens the rate limit. After five failures resp is still None, so resp.content raises an unhandled exception instead of a clean error. The correction classifies retriable vs terminal, uses capped exponential backoff that honors retry-after, and raises a named error or fallback when the budget runs out. The loop never reads retry-after.

question: A team must answer a broad market-research question that requires reading dozens of separate, unrelated sources. They are considering an orchestrator-worker setup. Why is this a good fit for the pattern?
options: The work splits into independent parts that subagents can explore at the same time
Orchestrator-worker always uses fewer tokens than a single agent on research tasks
Each step depends on the previous one, so a lead agent is needed to sequence them
Subagents share one context window, so they avoid re-reading the same sources
explanation: The pattern genuinely helps on large tasks that split into independent parts, such as research across many separate sources, because subagents explore at the same time. It costs more, not less, at roughly fifteen times the tokens of a chat, and each subagent has its own context window. Dependent steps are the case where fan-out does not pay off.

question: A single agent answers a typical question in about 10,000 tokens. A team rebuilds it as a lead plus four subagents, and Anthropic's reported multiplier applies. Later analysis shows most incoming questions were single lookups. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: Each question now costs about 50,000 tokens, which is justified by the faster response
Each question costs on the order of 150,000 tokens, and for single lookups that buys nothing
Token cost is unchanged, because subagents run in parallel rather than one after another
Each question costs about 150,000 tokens, which is always justified by higher answer quality
explanation: With Anthropic's roughly fifteen-times multiplier, a 10,000-token question becomes on the order of 150,000 tokens. If the question was a single lookup dressed up as research, four of the five contexts did work the task never needed. Parallel execution reduces wall-clock time, not token spend, and the multiplier's value depends entirely on whether the task needs the extra agents.

question: A team's research task really does benefit from orchestrator-worker, but the bill is high because every subagent runs on the top-tier model. Which adjustment does the course suggest?
options: Collapse the subagents into one agent, since fan-out is never worth its cost
Run the lead on a cheaper model and keep the top-tier model on every subagent
Use a more capable model for the lead and cheaper models for the subagents
Keep every agent on the top tier but cut each subagent's output tokens in half
explanation: The course suggests a more capable model as the lead and cheaper models for the subagents, so you avoid paying top-tier rates across every parallel context while keeping coordination quality where it matters. Collapsing to a single agent is right for tightly coupled work, but this task benefits from parallel exploration.

question: In an orchestrator-worker system, one subagent hits a rate limit, has no backoff, and fails silently. The lead agent stalls while it waits to compile results. What does this reveal about the design?
options: Orchestration replaces per-call failure handling, so the lead should simply time out
Only the lead agent needs retry logic, because subagents are short-lived calls
Rate limits cannot occur in subagents that run in parallel under one account
Each subagent needs its own retriable-versus-terminal handling, backoff, and fallback
explanation: Spreading work across agents multiplies the places a failure can occur, so each subagent needs the same retriable-versus-terminal handling, backoff, and fallback discipline, applied independently. The course says the orchestration pattern does not replace failure handling, it multiplies it, which is another reason to fan out only when parallel exploration is worth it.

question: A team lead asks why Anthropic's multi-agent research system outperformed its single-agent baseline on internal evals. According to the course, what was the main explanation?
options: Subagents use a special reasoning mode that a single agent cannot access
Token usage explained most of the performance variance, so the gain came from more parallel computation
The lead agent filtered out low-quality sources before any subagent read them
Multi-agent systems avoid context limits entirely, so no information is ever lost
explanation: Anthropic's analysis found that token usage accounts for most of the performance variance; the architecture works mainly because it buys more parallel computation. That is also why it costs roughly fifteen times the tokens of a chat. The course does not describe any special mode or source filtering behind the gain.

question: A team is reviewing an orchestrator-worker proposal before approving it. Which TWO statements about the pattern are accurate according to the course? (Select TWO.)
options: A runaway subagent or an oversized tool result can push cost well past the roughly 15x baseline
Parallel subagents always cut end-to-end latency because they add no coordination overhead
Parallel subagents can reduce wall-clock time on independent work but add latency to plan and compile
The pattern works best on tightly coupled tasks such as coding, where each step builds on the last
Because subagents share one context, the token multiplier applies only to output tokens
explanation: The multiplier compounds when something misbehaves: a runaway subagent or oversized tool result can push well past fifteen times. Parallel subagents can cut wall-clock time on independent work but add coordination latency for planning and compiling. The pattern is less effective on tightly coupled coding, and each subagent has its own context, so the multiplier applies to both input and output tokens.

question: A developer is about to ask an agentic coding tool to build a new production feature. What does the course recommend handing the tool before it writes anything?
options: A short prompt saying the feature must be production-ready
The repository and permission to iterate until the tests turn green
A list of the libraries it is allowed to import while it builds
A written plan with clear success criteria and explicit constraints
explanation: Plan the work first and capture it as a written artifact, then implement against it. A tool given clear success criteria and explicit constraints makes fewer assumptions and produces code you can check against the agreed document. Letting it iterate toward green tests skips the step where you define what correct means.

question: A manager proposes splitting every agent task into five parallel subagents to finish faster. Using the course's hiring analogy, when is hiring the team justified?
options: When the work splits into parts that can be done without waiting on each other
Whenever a task takes longer than a few minutes for a single agent to complete
Whenever the most capable model is too expensive to use for the entire task
When the task is a sequence of dependent steps that must be checked one by one
explanation: The course frames orchestration as a hiring decision: five researchers finish a broad survey faster than one, but you pay five salaries, so you only hire a team when the work splits into parts people can do without waiting on each other. Slowness alone does not justify fan-out; the fan-out case study shows a slow, dependent task getting a tripled bill.

question: Per-call logs show one step accounts for about 90% of a flow's spend: it stuffs full raw tool outputs into its prompt and makes redundant tool calls. Which TWO changes directly target that cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Trim the context and remove unnecessary tool output from the prompt
Enable streaming so the response starts arriving sooner for the user
Cut the redundant tool calls so the step makes only the calls it needs
Move every step in the flow to the most capable model available
Split the step across several parallel subagents to spread the load
explanation: Prompt and context size and the number of tool calls are both named cost levers: every prompt token costs money, and each extra tool call adds cost and latency. Streaming changes perceived latency, not cost. A bigger model or parallel subagents would multiply spend instead of trimming it.

question: Users of a chat feature complain it feels slow. Total generation time is about two seconds, and the team cannot shorten it. Which lever best improves how fast the reply feels?
options: Stream the response so the first tokens reach the user as soon as they are ready
Send the requests through the Message Batches API to lower the per-request cost
Add prompt caching to the user's message, since it changes on every turn
Fan the request out to parallel subagents so that each one writes a part of the reply
explanation: Streaming returns the first token as soon as it is ready; a response that starts in 300ms feels faster than one delivered as a block after two seconds, even with identical total time. Batching is the opposite trade, lowering cost by adding latency, and is wrong for anything a user is waiting on.

question: A team is planning where to place prompt-caching breakpoints in a high-volume assistant. Which TWO parts of the request are the best caching candidates? (Select TWO.)
options: The user's latest message, which changes on every turn
A long system prompt that stays the same between requests
A block of live account balances that refreshes on every request
A large tool schema that rarely changes between requests
A short ten-word instruction placed at the very end of the prompt
explanation: The components most worth caching are the ones that stay the same between requests, usually a long system prompt and a large tool schema. Content that changes every request never produces a hit and live data risks staleness. Short prompts fall below the model-specific minimum length, and content after the last breakpoint is processed normally.

question: A team assumes a lower-tier model is always cheaper and faster per request. In testing, a higher-tier model reaches a correct conclusion in far fewer output tokens on their hardest prompts. What does the course say about this case?
options: A higher tier is always slower and more expensive regardless of token counts
Token counts do not affect cost, so only the per-request price matters
A higher-tier model can be faster and cheaper if it reaches a conclusion in fewer tokens
The result suggests the eval is broken, since tiers never behave this way
explanation: The course notes that a higher-tier model can process a request faster and cheaper if it reaches a conclusion in fewer tokens than a lower-tier model would. Per-token price is only part of the cost, and the eval is the instrument for deciding. The assumption that higher tiers are always costlier is the shortcut the course warns against.

question: In a threat-modeling session, a team assumes an injection will eventually get past the model's training and the classifiers, and that the agent will act on it. What determines how bad the outcome is?
options: How carefully the system prompt warns the model about injected instructions
How many classifiers are layered in front of the model's context window
Whether the users who triggered the request are internal or external
What the agent's identity is allowed to do, which least privilege keeps narrow
explanation: Once a steered agent decides to act, the outcome is bounded by what its identity can do: with one output directory and read-only input, the injection becomes a denied action and a log entry rather than an incident. Prompt wording and classifiers reduce how often an injection lands but are probabilistic. That is why least privilege is the control that holds when the others fail.

question: An agent's configuration has three allow rules that would permit a write to /etc/hosts and one deny rule that forbids it. A PreToolUse hook also returns "allow" for the call. What happens to the write?
options: It is allowed, because the allow rules and the hook outnumber the single deny
It is blocked, because deny takes precedence over ask, which takes precedence over allow
It is escalated to the user, because conflicting rules always resolve to ask
It depends on which rule was added most recently to the agent's configuration
explanation: When multiple hooks or rules apply, the precedence is deny over ask over allow, so a single deny blocks the action no matter how many allow rules are present. That ordering is what makes the hook a real boundary rather than a best-effort check. Counting rules or using the most recent one is not how precedence works.

question: A healthcare customer with an existing zero data retention (ZDR) agreement wants the newest, most capable Claude model, deployed through a cloud provider. ZDR is a hard requirement. What should the team do during scoping?
options: Assume ZDR covers every model, since the customer's agreement is already in place
Confirm the model's ZDR eligibility in the Trust Center and check retention on that platform
Use the newest model and switch to an eligible one only if the security review objects
Skip the check for cloud deployments, since data retention is then the provider's concern
explanation: ZDR eligibility varies by model and platform and is not guaranteed even under an existing agreement; newer models may not yet have ZDR confirmed. Confirm each model's eligibility in the Anthropic Trust Center at scoping time and confirm retention on the platform too, which may constrain model or platform choice. Assuming the agreement covers every model is the trap.
